# Cast Iron Skillet

## Overview

I season with flaxseed oil, three very thin coats, baked at 230 C for one hour each. The trick is wiping the oil off like it was a mistake before it goes in the oven. Thick coats turn gummy, thin ones polymerise into a hard, glassy layer that lasts for years. I do the coats back to back on a Sunday, letting the metal cool between rounds, and it is ready for a steak the same evening. Cornbread and roast chicken are the two jobs it does best.

## Cleaning

While it is still warm but not hot I wipe it out with a cloth. For stuck bits I add coarse salt and a little oil, scrub with a folded rag, then rinse. I dry it on the hob over low heat for a minute so no water sits in the pores. A drop of oil spread with a paper towel keeps it ready for the next meal.

I never soak it, never leave it in the sink, and never put it in the dishwasher. A little soap is fine if I dry and oil it right afterwards. After a long braise I simmer a little water in it to lift the sugars, then carry on as usual. It lives on the hob, not in a cupboard, which keeps it dry and in reach.

## Troubleshooting

Sticky residue means too much oil went on last time or the heat was too low. Scrub it back to bare metal and re-season with two very thin coats.

Flaking black specks are a sign the seasoning bonded poorly. The cooking surface needs stripping back, then a fresh set of thin coats.

Rust spots come from moisture left sitting. Scour them off, dry the piece fully, and oil it while it is still warm.

Dull patches are just uneven seasoning and they cook fine. Keep using it and keep it dry, and the surface evens out over a month or two.
